register: wave-6 authoring register (S-B6 tranche) — part 1 of 2

items.stem: State the position a metal must occupy in the reactivity series before it will react with a dilute acid.
items.modelAnswer: The metal must sit above hydrogen in the reactivity series; metals placed below hydrogen do not react with dilute acids.

items.stem: Which salt family does sulfuric acid give with a metal, and which family does hydrochloric acid give?
items.modelAnswer: Sulfuric acid forms sulfate salts, while hydrochloric acid forms chloride salts.

items.stem: Explain why potassium and sodium are never used to demonstrate metal-acid reactions in school laboratories.
items.modelAnswer: Potassium and sodium sit so high in the reactivity series that they react with acids explosively, so the violent reaction would be far too dangerous to demonstrate in class.

items.stem: Equal-sized pieces of magnesium and iron are dropped into separate tubes of dilute hydrochloric acid. Predict the difference in what you would observe, and give the reason.
items.modelAnswer: Magnesium is the more reactive metal, so its reaction with the acid is the more vigorous: it fizzes faster and releases more heat, while the iron only bubbles slowly.

items.stem: List the products of a reaction between an acid and a metal carbonate.
items.modelAnswer: The products are a salt, carbon dioxide and water.

items.stem: State the general word equation for the reaction of an acid with a metal oxide base.
items.modelAnswer: Acid plus base gives a salt plus water: acid + base -> salt + water.

items.stem: Two white solids are added to separate samples of dilute hydrochloric acid. One mixture fizzes, the other simply stirs up with no gas at all. Explain what the fizzing reveals about the first solid.
items.modelAnswer: The fizzing is effervescence of carbon dioxide, so the first solid must be a metal carbonate: acid + carbonate reactions release CO2 gas, while a base such as a metal oxide gives no gas.

items.stem: Copper(II) oxide is added to dilute nitric acid until no more solid will dissolve. Name the salt in the solution and explain how the choice of acid fixed its name.
items.modelAnswer: The salt is copper(II) nitrate. Nitric acid always gives nitrate salts: the acid fixes the negative ion of the salt (nitrate), and the metal oxide supplies the copper(II) positive ion, so the two names combine as copper(II) nitrate.

items.stem: Which three metal specimens go into the test tubes in this practical, and in what physical form does each arrive?
items.modelAnswer: A length of magnesium ribbon, some iron filings and some zinc turnings — one metal specimen per test tube.

items.stem: Once the dilute hydrochloric acid runs are complete, what variation of the experiment is carried out next?
items.modelAnswer: The whole experiment is repeated using dilute sulfuric acid in place of the hydrochloric acid.

items.stem: Explain why the very first action in this practical is putting on safety glasses, before any acid is poured.
items.modelAnswer: Dilute acids are corrosive and can splash or spit once the metals start reacting vigorously, so the eyes must be protected before any acid is handled — the glasses go on first as a standing safety rule.

items.stem: During the magnesium run a gas is given off. Describe how you would test the gas and state the positive result.
items.modelAnswer: A lighted splint is held at the mouth of the test tube: hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop, so the positive result is the splint going out with a pop.

items.stem: Using the vigour of their reactions with the acids, state the order in which the three metals are placed.
items.modelAnswer: The order is Mg > Zn > Fe: magnesium reacts most vigorously, zinc reacts steadily, and iron reacts slowest.

items.stem: Name the gas and the dissolved product formed whenever any of these three metals reacts with a dilute acid.
items.modelAnswer: Hydrogen gas is given off, and a metal salt is left dissolved in solution.

items.stem: The three metals behaved identically towards hydrochloric and sulfuric acid. Explain what this consistency shows about the reaction pattern.
items.modelAnswer: The pattern is set by the metal's own reactivity, not by which acid is used: each metal reacts in the same way with both dilute acids, so the ranking does not depend on the acid chosen.

items.stem: A fourth metal X is tried under identical conditions and bubbles even more slowly than the iron did. Predict how X compares with iron in the reactivity series, giving your reason.
items.modelAnswer: X is less reactive than iron: reaction vigour falls going down the series, so slower bubbling under the same conditions means the metal sits lower — X ranks below Fe, though both still react.

items.stem: Define an alloy in terms of the substances it combines.
items.modelAnswer: An alloy is a mixture of a metal with one or more other elements — usually other metals, or a non-metal such as carbon.

items.stem: State the two metals present in brass and the percentage of each.
items.modelAnswer: Brass contains 70% copper and 30% zinc.

items.stem: Explain why alloys, rather than the pure metals they contain, are so often chosen for everyday objects.
items.modelAnswer: The blend often behaves differently from its ingredients: alloys can be stronger and harder than the pure metals, and many resist corrosion or withstand extreme temperatures, so they last longer in use.

items.stem: A bicycle maker wants a frame metal that shrugs off wet winters without rusting. Decide whether a pure metal or an alloy fits the need better, naming the property behind your decision.
items.modelAnswer: An alloy fits: many alloys resist corrosion, so a steel frame (iron mixed with carbon) withstands wet weather far better than a pure metal would.

items.stem: What does adding atoms of a different size do to the regular arrangement of atoms in a pure metal?
items.modelAnswer: It distorts the regular rows: the differently sized atoms spoil the neat arrangement of the pure metal lattice.

items.stem: How does the ease of layer sliding compare between an alloy and its pure metal?
items.modelAnswer: In the alloy the layers slide far less easily, and that difficulty is exactly why the alloy is harder than the pure metal.

items.stem: Explain, step by step, why the different atom sizes in an alloy make the metal harder.
items.modelAnswer: Atoms of different sizes distort the regular rows of the lattice, so the layers can no longer slide smoothly over one another; with slipping made difficult, the alloy resists shaping forces and is harder than the pure metal.

items.stem: An exam question offers four particle diagrams: A shows neat rows of equal circles, B shows uneven circles sitting in distorted rows, C shows molecules in pairs, D shows a fixed alternating grid. Which diagram represents an alloy, and what feature gave it away?
items.modelAnswer: Diagram B: uneven-sized particles in distorted rows are the signature of an alloy — the different-sized atoms have spoiled the regular lattice seen in the others.

items.stem: State which ions an acid forms when it is added to water.
items.modelAnswer: Acids form positively charged hydrogen ions, H+, in water.

items.stem: Classify a solution of pH 13 and name the ion it carries in abundance.
items.modelAnswer: pH 13 is well above 7, so the solution is alkaline, and it carries plenty of hydroxide ions, OH-.

items.stem: Explain why all acidic solutions, whatever acid made them, share the same core chemistry.
items.modelAnswer: It is the hydrogen ions, H+, that give a solution its acidity: every acid releases H+ in water, so the shared H+ ions give all acidic solutions their common reactions.

items.stem: A student tests three liquids: lemon juice, distilled water and oven cleaner. Predict their order from lowest to highest pH, naming the dominant ion in each.
items.modelAnswer: Lemon juice is acidic, so it has the lowest pH (rich in H+ ions); distilled water is neutral at pH 7; oven cleaner is strongly alkaline, so it has the highest pH (rich in OH- ions).

items.stem: Give, in ionic form, the single change that happens in every acid-alkali neutralisation.
items.modelAnswer: H+ + OH- -> H2O: hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions combine to give water.

items.stem: Magnesium reacting with hydrochloric acid makes a salt but no water. Does this reaction count as a neutralisation?
items.modelAnswer: No: although a salt forms, no water is produced, so the reaction does not fit the definition of a neutralisation.

items.stem: Explain why mixing hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide always ends in the same neutral product once the reaction is complete.
items.modelAnswer: Because neutralisation is the pairing of H+ with OH- to form water, H+ + OH- -> H2O; once every hydrogen ion has met a hydroxide ion, only neutral water (pH 7) and the dissolved sodium and chloride ions remain.

items.stem: A field's soil measures pH 5, but the crop to be planted cannot tolerate pH below 7. Name what the farmer should add and explain the effect on the soil.
items.modelAnswer: Add bases such as limestone or quicklime: they neutralise the acidic soil, raising the pH towards 7 so the crop can grow.

items.stem: State the proton-transfer definition of an acid.
items.modelAnswer: An acid is a proton donor.

items.stem: Give the ionisation of hydrochloric acid in water, naming both ions produced.
items.modelAnswer: HCl -> H+ + Cl-: hydrochloric acid ionises to hydrogen ions and chloride ions in water.

items.stem: Explain why the words proton and hydrogen ion can be used interchangeably when discussing acids.
items.modelAnswer: A hydrogen ion, H+, is simply a hydrogen atom that has lost its only electron — the particle left is exactly a proton, so the two names describe the same particle.

items.stem: Two different acids, hydrochloric and sulfuric, are each dissolved in water, and both solutions attack magnesium ribbon in the same way. Explain why different acids behave identically here.
items.modelAnswer: Each acid ionises in water, releasing hydrogen ions (protons), and the H+ ions are what make a solution acidic — the common H+ gives the common reactions with the magnesium.

items.stem: State, in proton language, the role a base plays.
items.modelAnswer: A base is a proton acceptor.

items.stem: Name the two ions formed when sodium hydroxide dissolves in water.
items.modelAnswer: Sodium hydroxide splits into Na+ and OH- ions.

items.stem: Explain why an alkali can neutralise an acid even though the base itself contains no protons at all.
items.modelAnswer: The alkali releases hydroxide ions, OH-, in water, and it is those hydroxide ions that accept the acid's protons: the base chemistry happens at the OH-, so the base needs no protons of its own — it takes the acid's.

items.stem: Hydrochloric acid is run into sodium hydroxide solution until the reaction is just complete. Describe the proton handover that has taken place, naming what each OH- ion has become.
items.modelAnswer: The acid played the donor role, giving protons (H+), and the hydroxide ions played the acceptor role: each OH- that accepted an H+ has become a water molecule, H2O.

items.stem: What is the natural source of litmus?
items.modelAnswer: Litmus is extracted from lichens.

items.stem: In what physical form is litmus supplied for dipping tests on solutions and gases?
items.modelAnswer: Litmus comes as red and blue paper for dipping into solutions or testing gases.

items.stem: Explain why litmus is passed over for titration work even though it distinguishes acids from alkalis perfectly well.
items.modelAnswer: Litmus passes through a purple transition colour at the changeover, so the endpoint is blurred; a titration needs a very sharp colour change to pinpoint the endpoint, which is why synthetic indicators are used instead.

items.stem: A student must choose an indicator that will show the endpoint of a titration unmistakably. Which family of indicators should be picked, and what property clinches the choice?
items.modelAnswer: Pick a synthetic indicator such as phenolphthalein or methyl orange: their colour change is very sharp, so the endpoint shows as an unmistakable colour switch.

items.stem: State the full range of the pH scale and the value that sits at its middle.
items.modelAnswer: The pH scale runs from 0 to 14, and pH 7 sits at its middle — the neutral point.

items.stem: What reference tool converts a universal indicator colour into an approximate pH reading?
items.modelAnswer: A colour chart: the indicator's new colour is matched against the chart, which gives the approximate pH.

items.stem: Explain why pH 1 is described as a stronger acid than pH 5, using the direction of the scale.
items.modelAnswer: The lower the pH, the more acidic the solution: pH 1 sits lower on the scale than pH 5, so it is the more strongly acidic of the two.

items.stem: A cleaner bottle is labelled pH 12 and a fruit-juice carton pH 4. Classify both using the scale bands and name the dominant ion in each.
items.modelAnswer: pH 12 falls in the strongly alkaline band (11-14), so it is rich in OH- ions; pH 4 falls in the weakly acidic band (4-6), so it is rich in H+ ions.
